scenes.visual: COLOUR MAP for both films (16:9, warm off-white background, flat cartoon style, no molecular structures): the SIZE LADDER is a tall vertical scale on the left third of the screen, rungs labelled 0.1 µm, 1 µm, 10 µm, 100 µm, 1,000 µm = 1 mm, 10 mm, each rung ten times the one below (log spacing, evenly spaced rungs). The EYE LINE is a thick BLUE horizontal line across the ladder at 100 µm, labelled 'eye line, 100 µm'. Cells are simple cartoon icons, always the same colour: frog egg = BROWN ball, Paramecium = TEAL slipper with a fringe of hairs, green alga = GREEN ball, red blood cell = RED disc pressed in on both faces, bacterium = AMBER short rod, cork boxes = TAN hollow squares. A 'picture' of a cell is a white rounded card holding that cell's icon, with its picture size printed under it. A microscope view is a white circle with a black rim. Any diagram not computed from the lesson's numbers carries a small corner label 'schematic'. Title card 'The Size Test' fades in over a glass jar of pond water that looks completely clear, lit from the side.

scenes.tts: This drop of pond water looks empty. Is it? And if tiny living things swim in it, why can't your eyes see them? To answer, we need one test of size.
scenes.visual: A single drop falls from the jar onto a glass slide and spreads. The drop looks clear. A large white question mark fades in beside it, then the drop slowly zooms toward the camera, still showing nothing.
scenes.narration: This drop of pond water looks empty. Is it? And if tiny living things swim in it, why can't your eyes see them? To answer, we need one test of size.

scenes.tts: Start with a metric ruler. Its smallest marks are one millimetre apart. Now split one millimetre into a thousand equal parts. Each tiny part is one micrometre.
scenes.caption: Start with a metric ruler. Its smallest marks are one millimetre apart. Now split one millimetre into a thousand equal parts. Each tiny part is one micrometre (µm).
scenes.visual: A wooden metric ruler slides in. The camera zooms into the gap between two smallest marks, labelled '1 mm'. The gap splits into 10 slices, then each slice splits into 10, then 10 again, with a counter reading 10, 100, 1,000. One last sliver glows, labelled '1 µm'. On screen: '1 mm = 1,000 µm'.
scenes.narration: Start with a metric ruler. Its smallest marks are one millimetre apart. Now split one millimetre into a thousand equal parts. Each tiny part is one micrometre (µm).

scenes.tts: Your eyes have a limit. Most people cannot make out anything smaller than about one hundred micrometres, a tenth of a millimetre. We will draw that limit as a blue line, the eye line.
scenes.caption: Your eyes have a limit. Most people cannot make out anything smaller than about 100 µm, a tenth of a millimetre. We will draw that limit as a blue line, the eye line.
scenes.visual: The 1 mm gap from the ruler reappears; a bracket marks one tenth of it, labelled '0.1 mm = 100 µm'. A cartoon eye beside it. The bracket stretches into the thick BLUE eye line, which slides left and becomes a horizontal line across an empty vertical ladder.
scenes.narration: Your eyes have a limit. Most people cannot make out anything smaller than about 100 µm, a tenth of a millimetre. We will draw that limit as a blue line, the eye line.

scenes.tts: Now build a size ladder. Each rung is ten times bigger than the rung below it. We place real cells on the ladder at their real sizes.
scenes.visual: The SIZE LADDER draws itself rung by rung from 0.1 µm at the bottom to 10 mm at the top, each new rung tagged '× 10'. The BLUE eye line stays fixed at 100 µm. Small empty slots appear beside the ladder, waiting for cells.
scenes.narration: Now build a size ladder. Each rung is ten times bigger than the rung below it. We place real cells on the ladder at their real sizes.

scenes.tts: A frog egg is one cell, often about a millimetre across. It sits above the eye line, so you can see it. A human egg, about one hundred micrometres, sits right on the line. A green alga, a red blood cell and a bacterium all sit below it.
scenes.visual: The BROWN frog-egg icon drops onto the ladder at 1,000 µm, above the BLUE line, with a small green tick and the tag 'often about 1,000 µm: you can see it'. Then the GREEN alga lands at 20 µm, the RED blood cell at 7.7 µm and the AMBER bacterium at 2 µm, each with its size tag and a grey 'hidden' tag, all below the BLUE line.
scenes.narration: A frog egg is one cell, often about a millimetre across. It sits above the eye line, so you can see it. A human egg, about one hundred micrometres, sits right on the line. A green alga, a red blood cell and a bacterium all sit below it.

scenes.tts: Most cells are somewhere between about one and one hundred micrometres. That puts most of them below the eye line, too small to see without help.
scenes.visual: A soft shaded band covers the ladder from 1 µm to 100 µm, labelled 'most cells'. The band sits just under the BLUE eye line. The alga, red blood cell and bacterium icons pulse inside the band.
scenes.narration: Most cells are somewhere between about one and one hundred micrometres. That puts most of them below the eye line, too small to see without help.

scenes.tts: A microscope uses lenses to make small things look larger. Magnification is how many times larger the picture looks than the real thing. So the picture looks as big as the real size times the magnification.
scenes.visual: A cartoon microscope slides in on the right. A dial on its side reads '1x'. Under the dial, the rule types itself out in large letters: 'picture size = real size × magnification'. It stays at the bottom of the screen for the rest of the film.
scenes.narration: A microscope uses lenses to make small things look larger. Magnification is how many times larger the picture looks than the real thing. So the picture looks as big as the real size times the magnification.

scenes.tts: Turn the dial up, and every picture slides up the ladder together. The cells do not change. Only their pictures grow. Watch the red blood cell. At forty times, its picture is already over three hundred micrometres. It has crossed the eye line.
scenes.visual: The dial turns 1x, 10x, 40x, 100x. With each click, a white picture card of every cell slides up the ladder by the same number of rungs (computed: picture = size × magnification). At the 10x click the RED blood cell's card reaches 77 µm, just under the BLUE line. At the 40x click it crosses the BLUE line; on screen: '7.7 µm × 40 = 308 µm'. At 100x it rises further, to 770 µm. Do not show the cells' insides; the cards only hold icons.
scenes.caption: Turn the dial up, and every picture slides up the ladder together. The cells do not change. Only their pictures grow. Watch the red blood cell. At 40x, its picture is already over 300 µm. It has crossed the eye line.
scenes.narration: Turn the dial up, and every picture slides up the ladder together. The cells do not change. Only their pictures grow. Watch the red blood cell. At 40x, its picture is already over 300 µm. It has crossed the eye line.

scenes.tts: Now the green alga, about twenty micrometres wide. Set the dial to just ten times. Will its picture cross the eye line?
scenes.caption: Now the green alga, about 20 µm wide. Set the dial to just 10x. Will its picture cross the eye line?
scenes.visual: All cards drop back to their real sizes. The dial snaps to '10x'. The GREEN alga icon glows; its card waits at 20 µm, below the BLUE line. A large question mark and the words 'Pause and predict' appear.
scenes.narration: Now the green alga, about 20 µm wide. Set the dial to just 10x. Will its picture cross the eye line?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame: alga card at 20 µm, BLUE line at 100 µm, dial at 10x, question mark pulsing. A thin countdown bar shrinks along the bottom.

scenes.tts: Yes. Its picture is two hundred micrometres, twice the eye line. The red blood cell, at the same ten times, still sits below the line.
scenes.caption: Yes. Its picture is 200 µm, twice the eye line. The red blood cell, at the same 10x, still sits below the line.
scenes.visual: The GREEN alga's card slides up and crosses the BLUE line; on screen: '20 µm × 10 = 200 µm'. The RED blood cell's card rises only to 77 µm and stops just under the BLUE line; on screen: '7.7 µm × 10 = 77 µm: not yet'.
scenes.narration: Yes. Its picture is 200 µm, twice the eye line. The red blood cell, at the same 10x, still sits below the line.

scenes.tts: A school microscope magnifies forty, one hundred or four hundred times. At four hundred times, most cells pass the eye line. Then you can see their shapes, if the lens shows them clearly and they stand out.
scenes.caption: A school microscope magnifies 40, 100 or 400 times. At 400x, most cells pass the eye line. Then you can see their shapes, if the lens shows them clearly and they stand out.
scenes.visual: The dial shows three settings, '40x', '100x' and '400x'. At 400x the cards of the alga, red blood cell and bacterium are all well above the BLUE line (computed: 8,000, 3,080 and 800 µm). The microscope circle fills with green balls, red discs and tiny amber rods; a small corner note reads 'shapes need a clear lens and a sample that stands out'.
scenes.narration: A school microscope magnifies 40, 100 or 400 times. At 400x, most cells pass the eye line. Then you can see their shapes, if the lens shows them clearly and they stand out.

scenes.tts: So a clear drop is not always empty. Most living things in pond water sit below the eye line, where our eyes cannot reach. That is why most cells stayed hidden until microscopes were made.
scenes.visual: Back to the drop on the slide. A microscope circle sweeps across it, revealing GREEN alga balls, AMBER rods and a TEAL Paramecium swimming and turning. Beside it the size ladder with the BLUE eye line stays in view, the shaded 'most cells' band just below it.
scenes.narration: So a clear drop is not always empty. Most living things in pond water sit below the eye line, where our eyes cannot reach. That is why most cells stayed hidden until microscopes were made.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex, the hexagon mascot, beside the ladder and BLUE line. Take-home line: 'Picture size = real size × magnification. Past 100 µm, it can show.'
